title: Wanting, being able to, having to
topic: querer, poder, tener que, deber + infinitive; asking politely
why: After verbs of movement and hacer, decir, poner, dar, here are querer, poder, tener que and deber, which let you say what you want to, can and have to do. The lesson sets up the ie and ue forms, the que in tener que, the negation trap, and the phrases for politely asking a favor.

Quiero, puedo, tengo que

With these verbs, you can say what you want to do, can do and have to do. They're followed directly by an infinitive, with no \"to\": Quiero salir (I want to go out), No puedo venir (I can't come).

querer (to want)poder (can, to be able to)tener que (to have to)deber (should, must)
yoquieropuedotengo quedebo
túquierespuedestienes quedebes
él, ella, ustedquierepuedetiene quedebe
nosotros, nosotrasqueremospodemostenemos quedebemos
vosotros, vosotrasqueréispodéistenéis quedebéis
ellos, ellas, ustedesquierenpuedentienen quedeben

The \"boot\"

Look at the forms in bold: the e of querer becomes ie, the o of poder becomes ue… except with nosotros and vosotros. If you circle the forms that change in the table, you draw a boot. English has nothing like this, so this shape is the easiest way to remember it.

The traps

  • I can = puedo, never \"podo\". We can = podemos, never \"puedemos\".
  • We want = queremos, without ie.
  • Deber is a regular -er verb: debo, debes, debe…

Querer also means \"to love\" someone: Te quiero (I love you). With an object or a dish, it means \"to want\": Quiero un café.

¿Quieres venir al cine? Hoy no puedo.Do you want to come to the movies? I can't today.
", "

Tener que or deber?

Good news: these two work a lot like English \"have to\" and \"should / must\".

UseExample
tener que + infinitivea concrete obligation, like \"have to\"; the most common form in speechTengo que trabajar el sábado.
deber + infinitiveadvice, moral duty, like \"should\" or \"must\"; a bit more formalDebes descansar.

Never forget the que, just as you never forget the \"to\" in \"have to\": Tengo que salir, never \"tengo salir\". And only tener is conjugated: Tenemos que esperar.

The negation

Here again, Spanish works like English. No tengo que trabajar means \"I don't have to work\" (it isn't necessary), not \"I mustn't work\". For advice or a prohibition, use no deber: No debes salir hoy (you shouldn't go out today).

SpanishMeaning
No tengo que ir.I don't have to go.
No debes ir.You shouldn't go (it's not a good idea).

To talk about an obligation, tener que is always the right choice in everyday speech. Save deber for advice.

Mañana tenemos que salir muy temprano.Tomorrow we have to leave very early.
", "

Asking politely

These verbs are mainly used to ask for things: permission, a favor, an invitation. Here are the phrases to know.

You want to…You say
ask for permission¿Puedo abrir la ventana? (can I open the window?)
ask a friend for a favor¿Puedes cerrar la puerta? / ¿Me puedes ayudar?
invite someone¿Quieres cenar con nosotros?
politely say what you'd likeQuería una información. / Quería reservar una mesa.
speak to a stranger (formal)¿Puede repetir, por favor?

¿Me puedes…?

¿Me puedes ayudar? means \"can you help me?\". Learn it as a set phrase: the little word me (me) goes before puedes, not at the end as in English. Same with ¿Me puedes esperar? (can you wait for me?).

Quería: the magic phrase

In a store or at a ticket window, Quiero… (\"I want…\") sounds a bit blunt. Spaniards say Quería… (literally \"I wanted\"), which sounds like \"I'd like\". It's a past form you'll study later; for now, take it as a ready-made polite phrase.

¿Puede repetir? is for someone you address formally: Spanish uses usted with the 3rd person singular for this. You'll see it in detail in the next unit.

Buenos días, quería un billete para Zaragoza.Good morning, I'd like a ticket to Zaragoza.
